To struggle means to try hard to do something that is difficult, while facing resistance or opposition.

That one sentence has three ingredients:

  • You are trying — you have not given up.
  • It is difficult — it is not easy or smooth.
  • There is resistance — something is pushing back against you, making it hard.

That resistance can come from outside you (a strong river current, a locked door, another person) or from inside you (a failing memory, fear, pain, weakness).
The Two Big Branches of Meaning

Branch 1: Physical Struggle

When your body fights against something forcefully, often to break free or push through.

  • A fish struggles on a hook — it twists and pulls violently, trying to get free.
  • A person trapped under fallen rocks struggles to get out.
  • Someone drowning struggles to stay above the water.

Here, the resistance is physical, and the effort is also physical — often involving urgent, repeated, forceful movements.

Branch 2: Non-Physical Struggle

When your mind, emotions, or efforts meet a challenge that is hard to overcome.

  • A student struggles to understand algebra.
  • A man struggles to forgive someone who hurt him.
  • A new business struggles to survive.
  • A mother struggles to hold back her tears.

Here, there is no physical fight, but the core meaning is the same: difficult effort against resistance.
The Key Prepositions That Change the Direction

The word "struggle" almost always points in a direction — toward something, against something, or to do something. The preposition you use tells you which direction.

Struggle to + [verb] — You are trying hard to achieve an action.

"She struggled to breathe." (Breathing was very difficult for her.)
"He struggled to smile." (Smiling took great effort.)

Struggle with + [noun] — You are having ongoing difficulty dealing with something.

"She struggles with loneliness." (Loneliness is a constant, hard challenge for her.)
"He struggles with his temper." (Controlling his anger is genuinely difficult for him.)

This form often implies a recurring or long-term difficulty.

Struggle against + [noun] — You are actively fighting in opposition to something.

"They struggled against the oppressive government."
"She struggled against the strong wind."

Here the emphasis is on the force you are opposing.

Struggle for + [noun] — You are working hard to gain or protect something.

"People struggled for their freedom."
"The child struggled for attention."

Here the emphasis is on what you want but haven't yet secured.

Struggle through + [noun] — You are pushing your way across a difficult path or situation.

"He struggled through the thick crowd."
"She struggled through a painful year."
The Essential Feeling Inside the Word

These four qualities are almost always present when someone "struggles":

1. Effort is real.
You are genuinely trying. You are not lazy or passive. If you give up completely, you have stopped struggling.

2. Success is not guaranteed.
If something is easy, you don't struggle with it. If success is certain, there is no struggle. Struggle lives in the uncertain, difficult space between trying and succeeding.

3. The difficulty is significant.
You would not normally say you "struggled" to open a bottle cap. You might say you "struggled" to finish a marathon, fight an illness, or write a book. The word carries a sense of real weight and strain.

4. Time is involved.
Struggling is rarely a one-second event. It usually involves sustained effort — minutes, hours, years. A person who "struggles with addiction" fights that battle over a long period of time.
Struggle Can Also Mean "To Move With Difficulty"

There is one extra, specific use: to struggle can describe moving through space when progress itself is the fight.

"The old man struggled up the stairs." (Each step was an effort.)
"The climbers struggled to the top in the blizzard."

This is still the same core idea — difficult effort against resistance — but applied to movement itself.

To make the meaning sharp, it helps to see what is not a struggle:

  • If something is easy, you don't struggle. You breeze through it, manage it, handle it.
  • If you are completely defeated and have stopped trying, you are no longer struggling — you have surrendered or given up.
  • If you try once and stop, that is not a struggle. Struggling implies repeated, sustained effort.
  • "Struggle" is not the same as "fail." A person can struggle enormously and still succeed in the end. Equally, they may fail. The word says nothing about the final outcome — only about the difficulty of the effort itself.
The Emotional Tone of the Word

"Struggle" is a serious word. It carries a tone of hardship, strain, and gravity. When you say someone is struggling, you are telling the listener that this person's situation is genuinely hard — and that they deserve some respect or empathy for facing it.

It is not a word used lightly. You would not say "I struggled to choose between chocolate and vanilla ice cream" in a serious sentence, because the difficulty is trivial. But you would say "I struggled to choose between staying in my country or leaving everything behind" — because that is a genuinely heavy, difficult effort.
A Simple Summary You Can Always Return To

To struggle = to keep trying hard at something difficult, while something pushes back and makes it hard.

The "something pushing back" can be a physical force, another person, a life circumstance, your own emotions, your own body, or the weight of the world around you. As long as you are still trying, and it is genuinely hard, you are struggling.
